```{r helpers, include=FALSE}
# Parse money text, including -£1,234, (1,234) and Unicode minus signs
parse_money <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(x, "[\u2212\u2013\u2014]", "-")
  neg <- str_detect(x, "^\\s*\\(.*\\)\\s*$") | str_detect(x, "-")
  num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(str_remove_all(x, "[^0-9.]")))
  if_else(neg, -num, num)
}

# Make financial year an ordered factor (chronological)
fy_factor <- function(x) factor(x, levels = sort(unique(x)))

standardise_columns <- function(df) {
  names(df) <- names(df) |>
    str_replace_all("\ufeff", "") |>
    str_squish() |>
    str_replace_all("Wind-up", "Winding-up") |>
    str_replace_all("wind-up", "winding-up") |>
    str_replace_all(" maximum budget available", " budget")

  # 24/25 splits constituency into two columns
  new <- "Constituency since 5 July 2024"
  if (!"Constituency" %in% names(df) && new %in% names(df)) {
    df$Constituency <- df[[new]]
    if ("Previous constituency" %in% names(df)) {
      df$Constituency <- coalesce(df$Constituency, df[["Previous constituency"]])
    }
  }

  # Drop the repeated "Reason for budget set" columns
  df <- df[, !str_starts(names(df), "Reason for budget set")]

  dupes <- names(df)[duplicated(names(df))]
  if (length(dupes) > 0) message("Duplicate columns after renaming: ", toString(dupes))
  df
}

load_series <- function(prefix, folder = data_dir, ...) {
  files <- list.files(folder,
                      pattern = paste0("^", prefix, "_\\d+_\\d+\\.csv$"),
                      full.names = TRUE) |> sort()
  if (length(files) == 0) stop("No files found for ", prefix, " in ", folder)

  frames <- map(files, function(f) {
    yr <- str_match(basename(f), "_(\\d+)_(\\d+)\\.csv$")
    df <- read_csv(f,
                   col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),  # everything as text
                   name_repair = "minimal",
                   show_col_types = FALSE, ...) |>
      standardise_columns()
    df$financial_year <- paste0(yr[2], "/", yr[3])
    df
  })

  # Flag any years whose columns differ from the first file
  base_cols <- names(frames[[1]])
  walk2(files, frames, function(f, df) {
    diff <- union(setdiff(names(df), base_cols), setdiff(base_cols, names(df)))
    if (length(diff) > 0) {
      message(prefix, ": ", basename(f), " column differences -> ", toString(diff))
    }
  })

  bind_rows(frames)
}
```

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
spend <- load_series("totalSpend")

# Keep only budget types present in the data
budgets <- budget_types[paste(budget_types, "budget") %in% names(spend) &
                        paste(budget_types, "spend")  %in% names(spend)]

# Convert every money column (budget, spend and remaining) to numeric in one pass
remaining_cols <- paste("Remaining", tolower(budgets), "budget")
money_cols <- c(paste(rep(budgets, each = 2), c("budget", "spend")),
                intersect(remaining_cols, names(spend)))
spend <- spend |> mutate(across(all_of(money_cols), parse_money))

# One tidy table (MP x year x budget type) that every plot and table builds from
budget_long <- map_dfr(budgets, function(b) {
  rem_col <- paste("Remaining", tolower(b), "budget")
  has_rem <- rem_col %in% names(spend)   # check before transmute creates a column called `spend`
  spend |>
    transmute(mp = `MP's name`, Constituency, financial_year,
              budget_type = b,
              budget    = .data[[paste(b, "budget")]],
              spend     = .data[[paste(b, "spend")]],
              remaining = if (has_rem) .data[[rem_col]] else NA_real_)
})

fy_range <- range(budget_long$financial_year)
```

# Overview

This document provides an analysis of MPs expenses using the "Total Spend" data from the [IPSA website](https://www.theipsa.org.uk/mp-staffing-business-costs/annual-publications). It has been conducted using methods in python and R and with the support of Large Language Models; any AI outputs have been thoroughly reviewed before use.

The data set in question outlines spend by MPs in conducting their work representing constituencies and this analysis provides an overview of what the data includes, any immediate trends or patterns of note and a series of further inquiries that are recommended to be investigated further.

# Executive Summary
- Preliminary high-level analysis has been conducted on MPs expenses over the financial years 10/11 - 25/26 with particular attention paid to 13/14 - 25/26 due to data quality differences in the early years.
- Spend associated with staffing expenses has significantly increased since FY 19/20 - approximately 50% increase over 5 years. Other budgetary items (Accommodation, Office, Start-up and Winding-up) showing no significant changes in the past 10-15 years.
- The vast majority of MPs remain under or within the budget each year with specific instances of overspend highlighted in more detail.
- Whilst spend related to staffing has seen a significant increase, the percentage of the budget being used appears to be dropping. This suggests extra available spend in each new budget is not always being used.
- A series of further inquiries have been highlighted including detailed review of overspend instances, checks on data quality and confirmation of why staffing spend has increased.

---

# Budget and Actual Spend

The data outlines spend against `r length(budgets)` categories (`r paste(sort(budgets), collapse = ", ")`); the first area investigated was the overall spend against budget.

```{r absolute-spend}
# Total budget and actual spend per category and year, summed across all constituencies
absolute_spend <- budget_long |>
  pivot_longer(c(budget, spend), names_to = "measure", values_to = "amount") |>
  group_by(financial_year, budget_type, measure) |>
  summarise(total = if_else(all(is.na(amount)), NA_real_, sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(financial_year = fy_factor(financial_year))

ggplot(absolute_spend,
       aes(x = financial_year, y = total,
           colour = budget_type, linetype = measure,
           group = interaction(budget_type, measure))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = ~ dplyr::filter(.x, measure == "spend"), size = 2) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(spend = "solid", budget = "dotted"),
                        labels = c(spend = "Actual spend", budget = "Budget")) +
  money_axis +
  labs(title = "Total spend and budget by category",
       subtitle = "All constituencies combined",
       x = "Financial year", y = "Total (£)",
       colour = "Budget type", linetype = NULL)
```
***Figure 1****: Plot of total spend across financial years for each budget category.*

This plot highlights that, over the years, spend for `Staffing` related expenses has been increasing with a significant up-tick in the rate of spend since 19/20; provisionally assumed to be COVID related and warrants further investigation given the ever-increasing rate since then. Other areas of spend have remained largely unchanged.

```{r overspend-data, include=FALSE}
# Every MP / year / category where remaining budget is negative
overspend_table <- budget_long |>
  filter(remaining < 0) |>
  mutate(overspend = -remaining,
         pct_spent = if_else(budget > 0, spend / budget * 100, NA_real_)) |>
  arrange(desc(overspend)) |>
  select(mp, Constituency, financial_year, budget_type,
         budget, spend, remaining, overspend, pct_spent)

# Percentage of budget used per MP, year and category
mp_usage <- budget_long |>
  filter(budget > 0, !is.na(remaining)) |>
  mutate(pct_spent = (budget - remaining) / budget * 100)   # >100 when remaining is negative
```

## Budget Control {.tabset}
The below tabs show budgetary over/under spend on an absolute and percentage basis as well as a table of every overspend instance. Click the different buttons to change between these views. There are `r nrow(overspend_table)` instances of budgetary overspend that can be identified in the "Overspend" tab.

### Absolute
```{r budget-variance-absolute}
# Total remaining budget per category and year, summed across all MPs
budget_variance <- budget_long |>
  filter(!financial_year %in% exclude_years_variance) |>
  group_by(financial_year, budget_type) |>
  summarise(variance = if_else(all(is.na(remaining)), NA_real_,
                               sum(remaining, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(variance)) |>
  mutate(financial_year = fy_factor(financial_year))

ggplot(budget_variance,
       aes(x = financial_year, y = variance,
           colour = budget_type, group = budget_type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  money_axis +
  labs(title = "Remaining budget by category",
       subtitle = "Sum of 'Remaining budget' across all MPs (below zero = overspend)",
       x = "Financial year", y = "Remaining budget", colour = "Budget type")
```

***Figure 2****: Budgetary over/under spend across all constituencies*

### Percentage
```{r ridge-function, include=FALSE}
plot_usage_ridge <- function(d, type, exclude_overspend = TRUE,
                             overlap = 0.6, bw = 0.3) {
  max_pct <- if (exclude_overspend) 100 else 120

  d <- d |> filter(budget_type == type, !is.na(pct_spent))
  if (exclude_overspend) d <- d |> filter(remaining >= 0)

  dens_df <- d |>
    group_by(financial_year) |>
    filter(n() >= 5, sd(pct_spent) > 0) |>        # KDE needs some spread
    reframe({
      dens <- density(pct_spent, bw = bw * sd(pct_spent),
                      from = 0, to = max_pct, n = 500)
      tibble(x = dens$x,
             height = dens$y / max(dens$y),         # same peak height for every ridge
             n = n())
    }) |>
    mutate(label = paste0(financial_year, " (n=", n, ")"),
           financial_year = fy_factor(financial_year),
           label = factor(label, levels = rev(sort(unique(label)))))  # oldest at the top

  ggplot(dens_df, aes(x = x, y = label, height = height, fill = financial_year)) +
    geom_ridgeline(scale = 1 / (1 - overlap), colour = "white",
                   alpha = 0.85, linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.15, end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, max_pct), breaks = seq(0, max_pct, 10),
                       expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(title = paste0(type, " budget: distribution of % of budget spent by MP"),
         subtitle = if (exclude_overspend) "Overspends excluded (remaining budget below zero)"
                    else "Overspends included (axis capped at 150%)",
         x = "% of budget spent", y = NULL) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```

```{r ridge-pct-spent}
plot_usage_ridge(mp_usage, "Staffing", exclude_overspend = FALSE)
```
***Figure 3****: Density plot of the percentage of budget spent by each MP over time. Note that a series of outliers are present where over 100% of the budget is spent.*

### Overspend
***Table 1****: All instances of budgetary overspend in any category.*
```{r overspend-table}
datatable(overspend_table,
          filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          colnames = c("MP", "Constituency", "Financial year", "Budget type",
                       "Budget", "Spend", "Remaining budget", "Overspend", "% spent"),
          options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)) |>
  formatCurrency(c("budget", "spend", "remaining", "overspend"),
                 currency = "£", digits = 0) |>
  formatRound("pct_spent", 1)
```

## {- .unlisted}

Several conclusions can be made on the above visualisations:

- Despite `Staffing` spend increasing, the amount of under spend against budget is also increasing suggesting continuous over-estimation of spend year on year.
- There a potential up-tick in over-estimation in recent years for `Office` and `Accommodation` expenses, however, more data would be required to draw a firm conclusion.
- There is an interesting feature in FY 15/16 where a significant proportion of constituencies only spent ~30-40% of their budget. This should be investigated further to confirm validity.

---

# Further Areas of Inquiry
This analysis provides a few areas that warrant further investigation:

- Confirmation that overspend data is accurate and not due to data quality issues.
- Understanding of what is driving the rapid increase in `Staffing` spend and budget despite a trend of under spend appearing since budgets have increased.
- Trend analysis of whether specific constituencies are likely to over or under spend on certain areas.
- Data quality review to confirm if the outliers of ~30% budget spend in FY 15/16 are valid.
